scenes.heading: Concurrency Pattern: Worker Pools
scenes.narration: Let's spend a minute on worker pools, Go's standard answer to processing many tasks in parallel without spawning unlimited goroutines.

scenes.heading: Why bound concurrency
items: One goroutine per task can spawn millions under load
A pool fixes the number of in-flight workers
Protects memory, file handles, and downstream limits
scenes.narration: Spawning a goroutine per task works until a load spike creates millions of them, exhausting memory or overwhelming a downstream database's connection limit. A worker pool launches a fixed number of goroutines that all pull from one shared jobs channel, so concurrency stays bounded no matter how much work arrives. That single decision makes resource use and throughput predictable.

scenes.heading: The worker-pool lifecycle
steps: Launch N workers ranging over jobs
Producer sends every task, then close(jobs)
Each worker's range ends when jobs drains
A watcher calls wg.Wait, then close(results)
scenes.narration: The lifecycle hinges on three rules. Launch a fixed number of workers, each ranging over the shared jobs channel and deferring wg.Done. The producer sends all tasks and then closes jobs, which ends every worker's range once the channel drains. A separate goroutine waits on the WaitGroup and then closes results exactly once, so the consumer can range over results and exit cleanly with nothing left blocked.

scenes.heading: A leak-free worker pool
scenes.narration: Three workers share one jobs channel, so the runtime load-balances work to whichever worker is free. The producer closes jobs after sending everything, which ends each worker's range. Crucially, a watcher goroutine closes results only after wg.Wait returns, guaranteeing no worker is still sending. The consumer ranges results until that close, and every goroutine has a guaranteed exit.

scenes.text: Size workers to the bottleneck: roughly GOMAXPROCS for CPU-bound work, the downstream limit for I/O; monitor queue depth.
scenes.narration: One last rule: more workers does not always mean more throughput. Size the pool to the bottleneck, roughly GOMAXPROCS for CPU-bound work, or the downstream concurrency limit for I/O-bound work. Keep buffers shallow so overload surfaces as backpressure, and monitor queue depth and goroutine count to catch leaks early.
